items.stem: What does defence in depth aim to achieve?

options.text: Multiple independent layers so one failure does not cause a breach
options.rationale: Correct: layered controls provide redundancy if one fails.

options.text: A single strong perimeter that needs nothing else
options.rationale: A single layer is exactly what defence in depth avoids.

options.text: Removing all internal controls once the firewall is set
Encrypting data only, with no other control
options.rationale: Defence in depth spans many control types.

items.explanation: Correct: layered controls provide redundancy if one fails.

items.stem: Which TWO statements reflect zero-trust principles? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Verify every request regardless of network location
options.rationale: Correct: zero trust does not grant implicit trust by location.

options.text: Grant the least privilege needed for each task
options.rationale: Correct: least privilege limits blast radius.

options.text: Trust any device once it is inside the perimeter
options.rationale: Implicit perimeter trust is what zero trust rejects.

options.text: Give all users administrator rights for speed
options.rationale: Broad admin rights violate least privilege.

items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Why segment a flat network into trust zones?

options.text: To contain an intruder and limit lateral movement
options.rationale: Correct: segmentation stops a compromise spreading freely.

options.text: To make every host reachable from every other host
options.rationale: That is the flat design segmentation replaces.

options.text: To remove the need for authentication
To increase east-west traffic without inspection

items.explanation: Correct: segmentation stops a compromise spreading freely.
